newsitem.title: GERMANY: Sketches of Bundesbank council members.
newsitem.headline: Sketches of Bundesbank council members.

text.p: Following are sketches of Bundesbank council members and what they stand for.

HANS TIETMEYER, 65, president whose term expires in August 1999. Tietmeyer, a Christian Democrat (CDU), is a top ally of Chancellor Helmut Kohl. Known as monetary policy centrist, he joined bank board in January 1990 after career in Bonn ministries. Named president in October 1993. He wants strict interpretation of Maastricht Treaty and has pushed for powerful stability pact. He believes Exchange Rate Mechanism membership is needed to join currency union and is critical of "window-dressing" finance measures to meet EMU criteria.

JOHANN WILHELM GADDUM, 54, vice president whose term expires June 1998. Gaddum, a CDU member and former president of the Rheinland-Palatinate bank, joined directorate in 1986 and appointed current job in October 1993. Also a centrist, he is an expert on capital markets but has limited international exposure. Gaddum is sympathetic to public's fears about the Euro and favours strict treaty interpretation. He favours stability pact with automatic sanctions and converting existing German debt into Euro as soon as possible.

OTMAR ISSING, 60, chief economist. Issing, a professor who has no political affiliation, joined council in October 1990 and is seen as a centrist on monetary issues. Issing is a proponent of the EMU stability pact and warns against softening EMU entry criteria. He also critical of "creative accounting" to meet fiscal criteria.

DIETER HAFERKAMP, 59, directorate member for personnel, trade settlement, risk control and safe custody accounts. Haferkamp, a lawyer by training, joined directorate on December 1, 1996. He worked as a lawyer before joining Bundesbank in 1968 and advanced in 1991 to head the legal department and then the personnel department in 1993. Haferkamp has made little public comment on Euro, other than to say effect on Bundesbank jobs would be initially modest.

WENDELIN HARTMANN, 59, directorate member for payment systems, controlling. Hartmann, a technical banking expert with no political affiliation, joined bank in 1964 and was appointed to directorate in June 1992. He chairs an EMI working group on coordinating cashless payments under EMU. Hartmann, an interest rate hawk, believes transition period between the Euro's introduction and physical distribution should be shortened.

HELMUT SCHIEBER, 58, directorate member for international relations. Schieber, who has no political affiliation, joined bank in 1964 and directorate in June 1992. Schieber, a centrist on rate policy, believes EMU target start date for January 1999 will be hard to meet and entrance criteria should not be relaxed. Selection of members should not be made before March 1998.

PETER SCHMIDHUBER, 65, directorate member for legal and administrative issues. Schmidhuber, a Christian Social (CSU) member, is ally of Finance Minister Waigel. Viewed as monetarist hawk, he joined directorate in March 1995. He believes timely start to EMU is possible if steps made to ensure stability. Delay could endanger project.

EDGAR MEISTER, 56, directorate member in charge of banking supervision. Meister, a Social Democrat (SPD), joined directorate in 1993 and considered favourite to replace Gaddum. Meister, a monetarist dove, wants clear interpretation of entry criteria. He cites public confusion due to questions about how criteria will be interpreted and fears political pressure may push through the introduction of the new currency at any price.

KLAUS-DIETER KUEHBACHER, 53, President of Berlin and Brandenburg state central bank. Kuehbacher, a former Bundestag member, viewed as outspoken SPD politician and expert on fiscal policy, named in September 1995 to current position. A monetarist dove, he wants EMU to start on time in 1999 with a small group of nations rather than risk delay or softening criteria.

FRANZ-CHRISTOPH ZEITLER, 48, President of Bavaria state central bank. Zeitler, CSU viewed as monetary centrist, appointed to post in 1995, oversaw in 1991 introduction of "solidarity surcharge" to pay for German unification. He is critical of nations using gimmicks to meet entry criteria.

REIMUT JOCHIMSEN, 63, President of North-Rhine Westphalia state central bank. Jochimsen, an SPD member and former professor, was economics minister of North-Rhine Westphalia before current position in August 1990. Jochimsen, monetarist centrist to dove, criticised France for budget moves, says Germany will not accept the Euro if the criteria are relaxed. Says Germany will be hard-pressed to meet the EMU budget goal.

HANS-JUERGEN KOEBNICK, 58, President of Saarland and Rheinland-Palatinate state central bank. Koebnick, a former journalist and SPD mayor, named president of Saarland bank in 1991 and Rheinland-Pfalz bank in 1993. A monetarist dove, he sees forecasts that Germany may miss EMU criteria in 1997 as realistic. EMU delay may be useful, and Italy, Spain and other "Club Med" countries unlikely in first group.

GUNTRAM PALM, 65, President of Baden-Wuerttemberg state central bank. Palm, a CDU member, was state minister before named to current job in April 1992. Palm, a monetarist hawk, warns against using tricks to join EMU. He favours criteria interpretation aimed at stability and wants stability pact.

ERNST WELTEKE, 54, President of Hesse state central bank. Welteke, an SPD member and former state economics and finance minister, was named to job in 1995. Welteke, a monetarist dove, believes any EMU delay to enlarge group unwise and could threaten project. Calls for strict interpretation of Maastricht targets, but stresses the treaty allows more leeway on deficit criterion than Finance Minister Theo Waigel has said it does. Waigel interprets the treaty as meaning that budget deficits can be no larger than 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.

OLAF SIEVERT, 63, President of Saxony and Thuringia state central bank. Sievert aligned with no political party, was professor before named to job in January 1993. Sievert, a monetarist dove, says EMU delay would be beginning of end, favours small group. Sees Euro helping solve European jobless.

HANS-JUERGEN KRUPP, 63, President of Schleswig-Holstein and Hamburg and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state central bank. Krupp, an SPD member and monetarist dove, was president of DIW institute. Named to current post in December 1993. Krupp says nations do not need to hit debt criteria exactly to qualify and sees room to manoeuvre, particularly on public debt.

HELMUT HESSE, 62, President of Lower Saxony and Bremen and Saxony Anhalt bank. Hesse, who has no political affiliation, is Club of Rome member. Was named bank president in December 1988 and given responsibility for more regional banks in November 1992. Hesse has made little public commentary on currency union. Considered a monetary centrist to hawk.
